title: Galaxy Galaxy, Burning Bright!
caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 3583, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, A. Riess et al.

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Two spiral arms twist outwards from the barred spiral galaxy NGC 3583 in this Hubble image. The galaxy lies 98 million light-years from the Milky Way, in the constellation of Ursa Major.

Two supernovae have exploded in NGC 3583, one in 1975 and a second, more recent one in 2015, though neither is visible. Supernovae can arise in a few different ways. Both of these came from binary star systems, pairs of stars in orbit around each other.

In each case, one member of the pair was a white dwarf, the leftover core of a Sun-like star. The white dwarf pulled material from its companion star and kept gaining mass until it reached a maximum limit. At that point it collapsed inwards and then blew apart in a brilliant supernova. The two explosions came from two separate binary systems within the same galaxy.

understand.summary: This image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, using filters at 350, 555 and 814 nm, from near-ultraviolet to near-infrared light. The colors assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Some of this light lies outside the range the eye can see, and Hubble shows structure in this distant galaxy that no eye could make out.
